title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
spaceBreakdown:
- int n, drops: two scalar variables → O(1)
- no containers, no recursion, no heap/stack allocations
- not counted: input vector nums
approach: A sorted-then-rotated array has at most one position where an element exceeds its circular successor. We count how many indices i satisfy nums[i] > nums[(i+1) % n]. If this count is 0 (fully sorted, no rotation) or 1 (one rotation break point), the array is valid; 2 or more means it cannot be a single rotated sorted array. This works because rotation moves exactly one "drop" from the end-to-start boundary into the interior (or leaves it at the boundary for zero rotation).
hints: In a fully sorted array, no element is greater than the one that follows it. How does rotating such an array change this property when you compare each element to the next, including the last element back to the first?
Count positions i where nums[i] > nums[(i+1) % n] (circular successor). For [3,4,5,1,2], the only such position is i=2 (5 > 1), so the count is 1.

```
count = 0
for i from 0 to n-1:
    if nums[i] > nums[(i+1) mod n]:
        count = count + 1
return count <= 1
```

**Single element** - n=1, trivially sorted
`Input: nums = [5]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: looping `for i in 0..n-1` and accessing `nums[i+1]` without modular indexing → out-of-bounds access at i=0

**All equal elements** - every adjacent pair is equal, zero drops
`Input: nums = [2,2,2,2]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: using `>=` instead of `>` in the drop check → counts 4 drops, returns false

**Wraparound is essential** - two drops exist but one is only visible with circular indexing
`Input: nums = [2,1,3,4]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: checking only `nums[i] > nums[i+1]` for i=0..n-2 without wraparound → finds 1 drop, returns true

**Already sorted, zero rotation** - the only "drop" is the wraparound from last to first
`Input: nums = [1,2,3]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: returning `drops == 0` instead of `drops <= 1` → finds 1 drop (3 > 1 at wraparound), returns false

followUps.q: What if you must also return the rotation offset x (or -1 if impossible)?
followUps.a: Scan for the single drop at index i; if found, x = i+1. If no drop exists, x = 0. If two or more drops exist, return -1. TC O(n), SC O(1).

followUps.q: What if nums.length can be up to 10^7 and the array arrives as a stream (one element at a time, no random access)?
followUps.a: Keep the previous element and a running drop count; compare each new element to the previous one, then compare the last element to the stored first element at the end. TC O(n), SC O(1).

followUps.q: What if duplicates are not allowed and you must verify the array is a rotation of a strictly increasing array?
followUps.a: Same approach, but use `>=` instead of `>` in the drop check so that equal adjacent pairs also count as violations. A valid strictly-increasing rotated array has at most one strict drop and zero equal pairs. TC O(n), SC O(1).
